reasoning: The claim that monosodium glutamate (MSG) causes headaches, numbness, and other symptoms collectively referred to as "Chinese restaurant syndrome" (or MSG symptom complex) has been debunked by extensive scientific research. The concept originated from an anecdotal letter published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1968. Since then, rigorous, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies conducted by health authorities, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA), have repeatedly failed to establish a causal link between normal dietary MSG consumption and these reported symptoms. The FDA classifies MSG as "Generally Recognized as Safe" (GRAS), noting that the body metabolizes glutamate added as seasoning identically to naturally occurring glutamate found in foods like tomatoes and parmesan cheese.
title: MSG causes headaches — 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'
